transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-02-05
Time: 15:00 - 15:48 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Lucas Ortiz (Redwood SE), Benji Park (CSM) — Priya Kapoor (CTO), Daniel Ruiz (NetOps), Sofia Martins (Cloud Eng), Tom Hsu (Security)

Summary:
Short sync to review last week's telemetry from the private pilot, validate the kernel upgrade candidate, and agree on next steps for the handshake/PSK test. Discussed routing heuristics, egress shaping and fallback policies, and outstanding security questions around KMS and logs retention.

Topics covered:
- Kernel upgrade (v2.3.1-rc) and compatibility with quantized weights
- Routing heuristics & circuit-breaker thresholds
- Telemetry gaps and span correlation for p95 spikes
- KMS handshake and audit log retention requirements
- Benchmark plan and next telemetry submission windows

Transcript body:
00:00 Maya Chen: okay welcome everyone uh thanks for joining, we have about 48 minutes today to go over the telemetry and the kernel candidate, um Lucas is going to run through the results and then we'll talk action items.
00:18 Lucas Ortiz: hey all, quick note, the kernel build we pushed last night is v2.3.1-rc, it's the one with the attention tiling fix and a small change to the kv cache eviction policy. it's low risk but we want to validate on Asterion's workload.
00:35 Priya Kapoor: thanks Lucas, on our end we saw a couple of p95 jumps during the late afternoon ramp, looks like around 14:20 local — I'm not sure if that's correlated with the batched prefix cache warmups.
00:52 Daniel Ruiz: yeah that spike matched a large burst from our webhook fanout, about 400 concurrent requests in 30s. we also had some packet retransmits on one of the interconnects but not sure if that's the root cause.
01:10 Lucas Ortiz: got it — two things there, one is routing heuristics: the pilot currently uses an even-shard routing for low-latency routes, when bursts happen we fall back to a batched pool which increases latency briefly. the newer heuristic adds a short-lived fast-path for re-entrant prefixes to avoid cold cache penalty.
01:38 Sofia Martins: can you explain re-entrant prefixes again? our team uses short prompts that often share prefixes so that would help, but we want to make sure it won't blow out memory on the GPU.
01:52 Lucas Ortiz: sure, basically if we detect X% of incoming requests share the same first N tokens in a rolling window, we keep their kv cache pinned in a fast-path pool for T seconds instead of evicting. memory overhead is bounded by pool size and we can configure it per model.
02:12 Tom Hsu: do we have an audit trail for when the pool is pinned and unpinned? we need to show for compliance when caches were retained and who triggered it.
02:25 Benji Park: good flag — currently we log pin/unpin events to the runtime trace, but we can push a higher-level audit event to the control plane so it appears in your compliance logs.
02:40 Priya Kapoor: excellent, that helps.
02:47 Maya Chen: Lucas, can you walk through the perf numbers from the last run? maybe screenshots or a quick readout.
02:56 Lucas Ortiz: yes — so overall throughput was within expected bounds, average latency was 28ms token latency for the small model, p95 spiked to about 420ms during bursts. we dug into spans and saw elevated application queue time. I'll share the trace link after the call.
03:22 Daniel Ruiz: queue time — is that inside the Redwood runtime or our side in the ingress LB? we saw 503 retries coming from one of our nodes.
03:34 Lucas Ortiz: mixed — a little of both. the runtime queue grows under sudden bursts if the fast-path isn't present. also if the customer's LB retries aggressively it amplifies the burst. recommended: tune your LB retry policy and enable the fast-path on the model.
03:50 Priya Kapoor: what's the recommended LB setting? we have an L7 proxy that retries on TCP timeouts.
03:59 Lucas Ortiz: set max retries to 1, add a 250ms initial timeout, and use exponential backoff. that avoids synchronized retries. we'll drop a config snippet.
04:16 Maya Chen: okay next, kernel compatibility — we've validated the quantized model on the RC build but want you to run the full suite. any red flags from security on the RC Tom?
04:28 Tom Hsu: quick read — the RC includes a new temp file handling routine, we need to confirm it uses secure tmp dirs and doesn't leak keys. also need to confirm KMS calls are done with mutual TLS and that audit logs include KMS request IDs.
04:44 Lucas Ortiz: yes, the build uses a secure tmpdir by default and KMS calls are mTLS. we can add the KMS request id to the runtime trace as an optional flag for your environment.
04:56 Tom Hsu: that would be helpful. also please include which ciphers are negotiable by the client.
05:07 Lucas Ortiz: will do.
05:12 Priya Kapoor: about fallback policies — when the private nodes reach capacity what's the recommended approach? we don't want to spill sensitive requests to hosted tiers.
05:26 Maya Chen: good point — Redwood supports routing policies per route. you can set a hard deny to hosted tiers for routes tagged sensitive, and configure a local degraded-mode response (short failover message) or queue longer in dedicated pools. we'll walk through recommended policies in the doc we share.
05:47 Daniel Ruiz: are those policies per-model or per-route? we have mixed traffic so ideally per-route.
05:54 Maya Chen: per-route. fine-grained.
06:02 Sofia Martins: telemetry: we noticed some gaps in span correlation across our ingress and Redwood traces — the trace IDs sometimes don't propagate. any suggestions?
06:15 Lucas Ortiz: we support W3C TraceContext and an SDK header we call x-rwd-trace that preserves the request context across the netpath. looks like your ingress strips unknown headers, we recommend allowing the x-rwd-trace header or using the W3C header which your network likely preserves.
06:36 Daniel Ruiz: we can patch the proxy, but is there a fallback mapping if header is missing?
06:42 Lucas Ortiz: yes, runtime will generate a synthetic trace id and attach a mapping in the initial event; that causes disjoint spans but we can post-process to heuristically join them if both ends have timestamps. better to preserve header though.
06:58 Priya Kapoor: perfect.
07:05 Maya Chen: turning to the kernel upgrade test plan, the recommended sequence is: smoke on a canary node, run 1 hour low load soak, then a scaled burst test (50k requests), then full-pool rollout if green. Lucas, can you outline the exact test harness?
07:25 Lucas Ortiz: sure — harness will replay recorded production ingress at 1x then 3x rates, capturing token latencies and KV cache hit rates. we'll instrument the run to emit detailed spans and a summary CSV. expect ~4 hours total for the scaled run but we can parallelize.
07:42 Priya Kapoor: can we do a short run today on a canary? we have a small window; it'd be good to smoke the RC.
07:51 Maya Chen: yes let's try to schedule a quick canary smoke after this call; Lucas can push the build and a script.
07:58 Lucas Ortiz: pushing now, I'll post the canary playbook link.
08:05 Daniel Ruiz: note: we have an egress policing SLA — if the kernel introduces additional small egresss for traces we need to check volume.
08:18 Lucas Ortiz: trace events are batched and compressed; the additional payload is minimal but we'll quantify it and provide delta numbers.
08:29 Tom Hsu: about logs retention — we have a 7-year retention policy for certain logs, not sure if that's realistic for the runtime traces.
08:38 Benji Park: we can export critical audit logs to your S3 with lifecycle policy; full runtime traces are heavier, but we can sample at 1% and export the rest to short-term storage. we'll document retention patterns.
08:59 Priya Kapoor: that sounds workable. please include estimated monthly egress.
09:06 Maya Chen: noted. Lucas, can you also clarify the pin/unpin audit events for the kv fast-path? we need the format to ingest into our SIEM.
09:18 Lucas Ortiz: we'll include timestamp, model id, route id, pool id, pin event, unpin event, and operator id — in JSONL format.
09:30 Sofia Martins: one more question on quantization — does the model change require re-signing in our model registry? we sign artifacts for provenance.
09:41 Lucas Ortiz: quantization is a transform we apply at serving time, the underlying artifact remains the same, but if you require a signed transform we can produce a hash manifest for the quantized variant.
09:55 Priya Kapoor: okay good.
10:02 Maya Chen: quick recap before we finish — action items are in the doc, next steps are the kernel build upload, run of the 50k sample benchmark and PSK handshake test next week. anything else?
10:17 Daniel Ruiz: can we add an extra telemetry tag for the LB node id to help correlate retries?
10:25 Lucas Ortiz: yes we'll add lb.node_id as optional metadata in the runtime events.
10:33 Tom Hsu: please add the cipher list and the KMS request id option.
10:39 Lucas Ortiz: noted.
10:44 Priya Kapoor: thanks everyone, schedule the follow-up for 2027-02-11 for handshake test.
10:51 Maya Chen: perfect, thanks all, we'll follow up in threads with links and the artifacts.

End of meeting.

Artifacts mentioned:
- Kernel build v2.3.1-rc (will be uploaded)
- Canary playbook link (to be shared)
- Perf harness & sample config (to be shared)
- SOC2 & KMS integration docs (to be shared)
- Trace link and CSV summary (to be shared after run)

Notes on transcript quality: medium — some proper nouns and acronyms may be slightly off, timestamps approximate to the nearest 10-20 seconds.
